bodyMarkdown:
## Before you start

Nothing beyond counting, though a drawn diagram helps enormously.

## The idea in plain language

Twenty students play cricket and fifteen play football. How many students are there? You cannot just say 35 — some of them play both, and you have counted those twice.

Subtracting the double-counted overlap once is the entire principle of inclusion-exclusion. Two overlapping circles on paper make it obvious.

## What is actually going on

For two sets: $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|$. You add both, then remove the overlap you counted twice.

For three sets the pattern alternates: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add the triple back. The triple overlap gets added three times and subtracted three times, so it needs adding once more to be counted at all.

When solving, fill the Venn diagram from the **middle outwards**. Start with the all-three region, then the pairwise-only regions, then the only-one regions. Filling from the outside in leads to double counting almost every time.

## Every question type you will meet

Each of these is a shape a question in this topic actually comes in. Learn to recognise the shape first — in a timed paper, picking the right method is most of the battle, and the arithmetic is the easy part.

### 1. Two overlapping sets

**Spot it when:** two categories with an overlap, and a total.

1. Use $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|$.
2. If some elements are in neither, subtract them from the total first.
3. Solve for whichever quantity is missing.

**Worked through:** 50 people, 30 tea, 25 coffee, 8 neither: $42 = 30 + 25 - x$, so $x = 13$ like both.

### 2. Three sets

**Spot it when:** three categories, usually with 'exactly two' or 'all three' mentioned.

1. Fill the diagram from the middle outwards: all three first, then the pairwise-only regions, then the singles.
2. Remember that 'both A and B' includes those who also have C, whereas 'only A and B' does not.
3. Use the alternating inclusion-exclusion formula as a check on the diagram.

**Worked through:** Exactly two $=$ (sum of pairwise overlaps) $- 3 \times$ (all three).

## Check yourself

You are ready to start practising this topic when you can:

- Apply inclusion-exclusion for two and three sets.
- Tell 'both' from 'only both' in a stem.
- Fill a Venn diagram from the centre outwards.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: In a class of 50, 30 like tea, 25 like coffee, and 8 like neither. How many like both?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Students liking at least one drink: $50 - 8 = 42$.

By inclusion-exclusion, $|T \cup C| = |T| + |C| - |T \cap C|$:

$42 = 30 + 25 - |T \cap C|$

So $|T \cap C| = 55 - 42 = 13$ students like both.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: Check: only tea is $30 - 13 = 17$, only coffee is $25 - 13 = 12$, and $17 + 12 + 13 + 8 = 50$.

formulaCards.title: Three sets
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: $|A \cup B \cup C| = |A| + |B| + |C| - |A \cap B| - |B \cap C| - |A \cap C| + |A \cap B \cap C|$
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: All singles 20, all pairs 8, triple 3 gives $60 - 24 + 3 = 39$.

formulaCards.title: Exactly one, exactly two
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Exactly two $=$ (sum of pairwise overlaps) $- 3 \times$ (triple overlap). Exactly one $=$ union $-$ exactly two $-$ triple.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: Pairwise 8 each and triple 3: exactly two is $24 - 9 = 15$.

commonTraps: Reading 'both A and B' (which includes people who also do C) as 'only A and B'.
Forgetting the people in none of the sets when the total is given.
Filling the diagram from the outside in. Always start with the innermost region.
